subject: Integrated Science
curriculum: KICD CBC 2021 (Junior Secondary School Curriculum Design, Grade 7)

sub_strands.title: Introduction to Integrated Science
kicd_learning_outcomes: identify the components of Integrated Science as a field of study
relate knowledge and skills gained in Integrated Science to career opportunities
appreciate the importance of Integrated Science in daily life
sub_strands.key_inquiry_question: How is the knowledge acquired in Integrated Science useful in daily life?
key_concepts: Integrated Science combines Biology, Chemistry, and Physics into one field of study
Biology is the study of living things — plants, animals, and microorganisms
Chemistry is the study of matter and how substances change and react
Physics is the study of forces, energy, motion, and how the physical world works
Knowledge from Integrated Science leads to career pathways in Senior School and beyond — including medicine, engineering, agriculture, and technology
kenyan_examples: Biology: understanding why a mango tree fruits each season, or how malaria spreads
Chemistry: why charcoal burns efficiently in a jiko, or how soap is made from ash and fat
Physics: how a matatu brakes suddenly, or how solar panels charge a phone in rural areas without grid electricity

qa_pairs.q: What are the components of Integrated Science?
qa_pairs.a: Integrated Science has three components: Biology, which studies living things like plants and animals; Chemistry, which studies matter and how substances react and change; and Physics, which studies forces, energy, and motion. Together these help us understand the whole natural world. What is one thing you did this morning that involved one of these three components?

qa_pairs.q: How can knowledge from Integrated Science lead to a career?
qa_pairs.a: Integrated Science builds the foundation for many careers in Senior School and beyond — Biology leads toward medicine, nursing, or agriculture; Chemistry leads toward pharmacy or industrial chemistry; Physics leads toward engineering or aviation. The scientific thinking skills you build now, like observing carefully and testing ideas, are useful in almost every career, even ones that don't seem like science at first. What career are you curious about, and which part of science do you think it connects to?

qa_pairs.q: Why is Integrated Science important in daily life?
qa_pairs.a: Integrated Science helps us make informed choices every day — from understanding why we need to wash our hands to prevent illness, to knowing why food spoils, to understanding how a phone charger works. Farmers use it to grow better crops, doctors use it to treat patients, and engineers use it to build safer roads. Without scientific understanding, many everyday problems would be much harder to solve. Can you name one decision you made today that used scientific thinking, even without realising it?

sub_strands.title: Laboratory Safety
kicd_learning_outcomes: identify common hazards and their symbols in the laboratory
analyse causes of common accidents in the laboratory
demonstrate first aid safety measures for common laboratory accidents
appreciate the importance of safety and access to a healthy working environment
key_inquiry_questions: How do accidents happen in the laboratory?
What safety measures should be considered while constructing a laboratory?
key_concepts: Hazard symbols are pictures that warn of danger before you touch a substance — recognised instantly regardless of language
Flammable symbol (orange flame): the substance catches fire very easily — keep away from heat and sparks
Corrosive symbol: the substance burns and damages skin and materials on contact
Toxic symbol (skull and crossbones): the substance can cause serious harm or death if swallowed, inhaled, or touched
Carcinogenic symbol: the substance may cause cancer with repeated or prolonged exposure
Radioactive symbol: the substance emits radiation that can be harmful with unsafe exposure
First aid for burns and scalds: run cool water over the area for several minutes — never apply toothpaste, butter, or oil
First aid for cuts: apply firm pressure with a clean cloth and seek assistance
First aid for ingestion of harmful substances: do not induce vomiting — seek immediate help
Safety in the laboratory protects both the individual and the people working around them
kenyan_examples: Corrosive: car battery acid (sulphuric acid) — mechanics wear gloves when handling batteries for this reason
Flammable: petrol at a fuel station — this is why smoking is banned near fuel pumps
Toxic: agricultural pesticides used on farms — always stored away from children and food

Radioactive and carcinogenic hazards are rarer in a school lab but appear on some industrial and medical waste containers, which is why the symbol itself, not just the substance, must always be respected

qa_pairs.q: What does the flammable hazard symbol mean, and where might you see it in Kenya?
qa_pairs.a: The flammable symbol shows an orange flame. It warns that a substance catches fire very easily and must be kept away from heat, sparks, and open flames. You see this symbol on petrol containers and cooking gas cylinders — which is exactly why fuel stations in Kenya do not allow smoking near the pumps. If you saw this symbol on a bottle in the school laboratory, what would you do differently while handling it?

qa_pairs.q: What is the correct first aid response for a burn in the laboratory?
qa_pairs.a: Immediately run cool water over the burn for several minutes. Never apply toothpaste, butter, or oil — these trap heat and can make the injury worse. If it is safe, remove nearby jewellery or tight clothing, then cover the burn loosely with a clean cloth and inform your teacher right away. Cool water is the only correct first response for a burn. Why do you think people sometimes reach for something like toothpaste out of habit, even though it does not help?

qa_pairs.q: What should you do if a classmate accidentally swallows a laboratory chemical?
qa_pairs.a: Do not try to make them vomit — this can burn the throat a second time on the way back up. Seek help immediately from a teacher and get medical attention without delay. Checking the container for its hazard symbol quickly tells you how serious the danger might be — a skull and crossbones means it is toxic and needs urgent care. Why do you think hazard symbols need to be understood before an accident happens, not looked up during one?

qa_pairs.q: Why does a laboratory need clear safety rules, not just careful individual behaviour?
qa_pairs.a: A laboratory is a shared working environment — one person's mistake, like leaving a flammable substance near a heat source, can put everyone in the room at risk, not just themselves. Safety rules exist so that everyone knows what to expect from each other, the same way traffic rules protect everyone on the road, not just careful drivers. This is why laboratory safety is both a personal responsibility and a shared one. Can you think of a rule at home that exists to protect the whole family, not just one person?

sub_strands.title: Basic Science Skills
kicd_learning_outcomes: use the International System of Units (SI) for basic and derived quantities in science
appreciate the application of basic skills in science
key_inquiry_questions: How are basic skills in science important in daily life?
key_concepts: The basic skills in science are: manipulative, observation, measurement, classification, prediction, communication, and conclusion skills
Manipulative skills involve correctly handling apparatus and materials during an investigation
Observation skills involve noticing details carefully using the senses
Measurement skills involve using instruments correctly to collect accurate data
Classification skills involve grouping things based on shared characteristics
Prediction skills involve making an informed guess about what will happen, based on evidence
Communication skills involve clearly sharing findings, in writing, speech, or diagrams
Conclusion skills involve interpreting results and stating what they mean
SI units are the internationally agreed standard units for quantities like temperature, length, mass, time, electric current, area, volume, and density
Reading packing labels on products is a real-life application of understanding quantities and units
kenyan_examples: A market trader weighing maize or beans in kilograms uses the same measurement principle as a scientist using a scale in the lab
Reading the net weight on a packet of unga or the volume on a bottle of cooking oil is a direct, everyday use of understanding units
A boda boda rider estimating fuel needed for a trip uses prediction skills grounded in past experience and observation

qa_pairs.q: What are the basic skills used in scientific investigation?
qa_pairs.a: The basic science skills are manipulative skills, which means handling apparatus correctly; observation skills, noticing details carefully; measurement skills, using instruments accurately; classification skills, grouping things by shared features; prediction skills, making informed guesses based on evidence; communication skills, sharing findings clearly; and conclusion skills, interpreting what results actually mean. Which of these skills do you think you already use without realising it, even outside of science class?

qa_pairs.q: Why is it important to read packing labels on products?
qa_pairs.a: Packing labels tell you the exact quantity of what you are buying, using standard units — for example, the net weight in grams on a packet of unga, or the volume in millilitres on a bottle of cooking oil. Understanding these units helps you compare products fairly, know if you are getting the right amount, and even calculate value for money. This is a direct, everyday application of the same measurement skills used in a science laboratory. Next time you are at a shop, what is one product where checking the label might change your buying decision?

qa_pairs.q: Why do scientists everywhere use the same SI units?
qa_pairs.a: SI units are internationally agreed standards, meaning a measurement taken in a laboratory in Nairobi means exactly the same thing as one taken in Tokyo or London. This allows scientists worldwide to compare results accurately and trust each other's data. If every country used different units, sharing and verifying scientific findings would become very difficult. Can you think of a problem that could happen if two people used different units to measure the same thing?

sub_strands.title: Laboratory Apparatus and Instruments
kicd_learning_outcomes: identify apparatus and instruments used in the laboratory
handle and care for the apparatus and instruments in the laboratory
appreciate the importance of consumer protection when handling different apparatus and chemicals in the laboratory
key_inquiry_questions: What are the uses of different laboratory apparatus and instruments?
What are the basic measures that should be considered when storing different laboratory apparatus?
key_concepts: Laboratory apparatus and instruments are used for heating, measuring mass, temperature, length, volume, weight, magnification, and time
A microscope is used to magnify very small objects — its main parts include the eyepiece, objective lens, stage, and light source
A Bunsen burner is used for heating and has parts including the barrel, air hole, and gas inlet
A beaker is used to hold, mix, or heat liquids — its volume markings are approximate, not precise
A measuring cylinder gives an accurate liquid volume reading, read at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus
A thermometer measures temperature, typically in degrees Celsius in Kenyan school laboratories
A triple beam balance or digital scale measures mass, in grams or kilograms
Correct handling and storage of apparatus prevents damage, breakage, and accidents
Consumer protection means using and storing chemicals and apparatus responsibly to avoid harming yourself, others, or the environment
kenyan_examples: A market trader's weighing scale mirrors the principle of a laboratory triple beam balance
A clinical thermometer used at a local dispensary works on the same principle as a laboratory thermometer
Careful storage of farm chemicals at home, away from children and food, reflects the same consumer protection principle used for laboratory chemicals

qa_pairs.q: What is the difference between a beaker and a measuring cylinder?
qa_pairs.a: A beaker is mainly used for mixing, holding, or heating liquids, and its volume markings are only approximate. A measuring cylinder is specifically designed for accurate volume measurement, and you always read it at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus, the curved surface of the liquid. If you needed exactly 50 millilitres of water for an experiment, which apparatus should you use, and why?

qa_pairs.q: What are the main parts of a microscope, and what is it used for?
qa_pairs.a: A microscope is used to magnify very small objects that cannot be seen clearly with the naked eye. Its main parts include the eyepiece, which you look through; the objective lens, which magnifies the specimen; the stage, where the specimen sits; and the light source, which illuminates it. Scientists and doctors use microscopes to study cells, identify microorganisms, and diagnose diseases. What is one small object you have seen that you think would look completely different under a microscope?

qa_pairs.q: Why is proper handling and storage of laboratory apparatus important?
qa_pairs.a: Proper handling prevents breakage, accidents, and waste of resources — a dropped beaker cannot be reused, and a poorly stored chemical can become a safety hazard for the next person who uses the lab. This connects to consumer protection: taking responsibility for equipment protects not just you, but everyone who uses the laboratory after you. Just like storing farm chemicals safely at home protects the whole family, proper laboratory storage protects the whole class. Can you think of an item at home that needs careful storage to stay safe or usable?
